items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Atomic spectra: inverses, not energy gaps
items.concept: Hydrogenic emission uses 1/λ = R(1/n_low²−1/n_high²). A larger energy or wavenumber gap means a shorter wavelength; always choose n_high greater than n_low.
items.predict: Will the 4→2 Balmer photon have a shorter or longer wavelength than the 3→2 photon? Predict before evaluating fractions.
items.challenge: Independently find λ(5→2)/λ(4→2) for a hydrogen-like atom. Show the inverse-ratio logic; numerical R is unnecessary.
steps: For 4→2 the factor is 3/16. Invert factors for wavelengths: λ(5→2)/λ(4→2)=(3/16)/(21/100)=25/28≈0.893.
The 5→2 transition emits the shorter wavelength because its level gap is larger.
items.trap: Using the ratio of energy gaps as though it were the ratio of wavelengths.
items.repair: Write each wavenumber factor, put λ proportional to its reciprocal, then compare the resulting ratio and inequality.
items.boundary: Would an n=2→n=2 transition yield a spectral line?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Its level-energy difference is zero; the line formula yields zero wavenumber, not a finite emitted photon.

items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Amphoteric oxides and equivalent bookkeeping
items.concept: Amphoteric ZnO reacts with both acid and excess strong alkali. Balance the atoms and charge before applying a mole ratio. With acid, ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O.
items.predict: Would adding twice as many moles of HCl as ZnO be sufficient for complete acid dissolution? State the stoichiometric reason.
items.worked: 4.07 g of ZnO at molar mass 81.4 g/mol is 0.050 mol. Its acid dissolution needs 0.100 mol HCl, not 0.050 mol.
items.challenge: A clean 8.14 g sample of ZnO reacts with HCl. Calculate the minimum amount of HCl in moles and the volume of 0.50 M HCl solution needed.
steps: n(ZnO)=8.14/81.4=0.100 mol, using the molar mass of ZnO and the measured sample mass.
The balanced equation needs 2 mol HCl per mol ZnO, hence n(HCl)=0.200 mol.
items.trap: Using a 1:1 ratio because the oxide formula contains one zinc atom.
items.repair: Mark the coefficient 2 in the balanced reaction and write mole-needed = coefficient × limiting-reactant moles.
items.boundary: If only 0.10 mol HCl is available for this 8.14 g sample, can all of the ZnO dissolve?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Only 0.050 mol ZnO can react with 0.10 mol HCl; the remaining 0.050 mol ZnO is unreacted under this acid-only model.

items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Gas-volume conservation in combustion eudiometry
items.concept: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes follow stoichiometric mole ratios. In CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, water is condensed before reading the dry gas; an alkali absorbent can then remove CO2.
items.predict: After burning methane in excess oxygen and condensing water, is the remaining dry gas necessarily only carbon dioxide?
items.worked: 15 mL CH4 consumes 30 mL O2, leaving 5 mL from an initial 35 mL O2. It produces 15 mL CO2: dry residual gas =20 mL; after CO2 absorption, 5 mL remains.
items.challenge: Burn 12 mL CH4 with 30 mL O2 at the same gas conditions. Determine the dry volume after water condenses and the final volume after removing CO2 with alkali.
steps: Required O2 is twice methane: 24 mL, leaving 30−24=6 mL O2.
CO2 formed is 12 mL; after condensing water, dry volume =12+6=18 mL.
An alkaline absorber removes 12 mL CO2, leaving 6 mL O2.
items.trap: Counting water vapour as dry gas or subtracting CO2 before calculating oxygen excess.
items.repair: Write three separate columns: reacted volume, dry gas after condensation, and gas after selective CO2 absorption.
items.boundary: If oxygen supplied were only 20 mL for 12 mL methane, could all methane burn completely?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Complete combustion needs 24 mL oxygen; the mixture is oxygen-limited and cannot be evaluated with the all-methane-complete assumption.

items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Mole fraction and partial pressures
items.concept: For an ideal nonreacting gas mixture at equilibrium, Dalton's law is p_i = x_i P_total, where x_i=n_i/Σn. Mole fractions must sum to one.
items.predict: Can a minority gas by mole count have a larger partial pressure than a majority gas under identical ideal mixing conditions?
items.worked: In a vessel with 2 mol N2 and 3 mol O2 at total pressure 5 atm, x_N2=2/5 and x_O2=3/5, yielding p_N2=2 atm and p_O2=3 atm.
items.challenge: A 10-atm ideal mixture contains 1 mol helium and 4 mol neon. Calculate each partial pressure, then check whether they sum to total pressure.
steps: Total moles are 1+4=5; x_He=1/5 and x_Ne=4/5.
Apply Dalton's law: p_He=(1/5)×10=2 atm and p_Ne=(4/5)×10=8 atm.
Check p_He+p_Ne=10 atm; each partial pressure is nonnegative and ≤ total.
items.trap: Using molar mass or an arbitrary volume fraction when the ideal mixture is specified by mole numbers.
items.repair: Find the total moles first, then normalize each component amount before multiplying by total pressure.
items.boundary: Would the same simple partial-pressure rule remain valid if gases react appreciably before measurement?
items.boundaryAnswer: Not with the initial unreacted mole numbers. First determine equilibrium compositions; only then use the relevant mixture relations.

items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Redox titration by electron-equivalent balance
items.concept: In acidic solution, MnO4− takes 5 electrons to become Mn²⁺, whereas Fe²⁺ donates one electron to become Fe³⁺. Balance exchanged electron-moles before titration arithmetic.
items.predict: Does one mole of acidic permanganate oxidise one mole or five moles of Fe²⁺? Explain the electron count.
items.worked: 20 mL of 0.020 M KMnO4 contains 0.00040 mol permanganate and can oxidise 5×0.00040=0.00200 mol Fe²⁺ in acid.
items.challenge: 25.0 mL of 0.0100 M acidic KMnO4 reaches the equivalence point with Fe²⁺. Determine the Fe²⁺ amount in moles and the 0.0500 M Fe²⁺ solution volume consumed.
steps: Five Fe²⁺ donate the five electrons needed per permanganate; n(Fe²⁺)=1.25×10⁻³ mol.
items.trap: Assuming a one-to-one mole ratio without considering the oxidation-state changes.
items.repair: Balance the oxidation/reduction half-reactions first and then use n oxidant×n-factor = n reductant×n-factor.
items.boundary: Would the same five-electron permanganate reduction necessarily apply in strongly alkaline solution?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. The Mn product and electron stoichiometry depend on medium; confirm the reaction product and rebalance for that environment.
